info.name: shortlinkQr-API
info.description:
Functional test collection for the shortlinkQr API.

The collection is organised in six folders:

1. Links API - the happy paths of the management endpoints.
2. Validation - requests that must be rejected by Bean Validation with 400 and a per-field `errors` map.
3. Protocol errors - malformed or unsupported requests handled by ResponseEntityExceptionHandler.
4. Redirect - the public endpoint a scanned QR code hits.
5. QR & Logo - the endpoint for check add image to a previous QR.
6. Authorization & edition - managing the link via PATCH and asserting token validation.

Every request carries a test script asserting the expected status, so the whole collection can be executed with the Collection Runner and read as a pass/fail report.

Variables:
- baseUrl: host of the running application (default http://localhost:9080)
- lastCode: filled automatically by the first request, so later requests need no manual copying.
- aliasCode: the custom alias used to exercise the conflict case.
- managementToken: captured token to authenticate edit and inspection endpoints.
- plainQrSize: stored size of the unbranded QR code.

exec: pm.test('both violations are merged into one entry', () => {

request.description:
Two characters and an illegal one, so @Size and @Pattern both fail on the same field.

This is the request that exercises the merge function of Collectors.toMap. Without it, collecting two violations under one key throws IllegalStateException and the 400 turns into a 500.

The assertions check for substrings rather than the whole message: Bean Validation does not guarantee the order in which constraints on one field are evaluated.

item.name: 4. Redirect

request.description: 301 would let browsers cache the destination permanently, so a printed QR code could never be re-pointed. The status assertion is the regression guard for the project's core promise.

Run straight after 20. Reads the same link through the management endpoint to confirm the redirect incremented the counter.

Together with request 05 this pins both halves of the rule: resolving counts, inspecting does not.
Known limitation: a person who scans a dead QR code receives an RFC 7807 JSON document in their browser. Correct for an API, poor for a human. An HTML error page for this endpoint is pending.

item.name: 23 - Path that cannot be a code

exec: pm.test('handled as a missing resource, not as a missing link', () => {

request.description:
The path variable is constrained to the shape of a code, so requests that cannot possibly be one never reach the service or the database.

This matters because the redirect endpoint sits at the site root: without the constraint, every scanner probing for /wp-admin or /.env would cost a query.

request.description:
Same URL as request 24, different bytes. The size comparison is the cheapest assertion that proves the branch was taken: the plain symbol is written from a one-bit canvas, the branded one from TYPE_INT_RGB, so it is reliably larger.

It is also why this endpoint can no longer promise immutable.

item.name: 6. Authorization & edition

exec: pm.test('managementToken is not returned on edition', () => pm.expect(body.managementToken).to.be.undefined);

request.description:
The project's whole premise in one request: the printed symbol stays valid while the destination changes. The QR encodes the short link, not the target, so re-pointing a link leaves every printed copy working.

Run with the token captured by request 01. From here on the link resolved by request 20 points somewhere else.

A link created without an expiry can gain one later. Only the field that arrives is applied, so the destination set by request 29 survives untouched - an absent field means "leave it alone", never "set it to null".

Depends on request 30 having run: without a date to remove, asserting null would pass without the flag doing anything.

A null expiry already means "never expires", so the protocol cannot express the transition to that state by sending null - absent and null both mean "leave it alone". The clearExpiry flag is what carries the intent, which is why no sentinel date was used: 9999-12-31 is not perpetual, it expires in 7973 years.

403 and not 401: there is no identity to authenticate, so a WWW-Authenticate challenge would have nothing to ask for. The system has resources and no principals, and possession of the capability is the entire credential.

A missing header is rejected by the same path as a wrong one, so the response cannot be used to tell the two apart.

exec: pm.test('the failing code is not returned to an unauthorised caller', () => {

request.description:
The stored value is a SHA-256 digest and the comparison is constant-time, so a near-miss costs the same as a wild guess. A null stored hash denies: the guard fails closed.

Unlike the 404, this response carries no `code` property. The failing code goes to the log, where the owner of the service can see it, and not to a caller who has just proved they are not the owner of the link.

An empty object is not an empty body. `{}` is readable, so it binds with every field absent, a derived @AssertTrue method fires, and the failure arrives through the same MethodArgumentNotValidException path as any other validation error - with the per-field `errors` map.

An unreadable body is a different exception and a 400 without that map.

item.name: 35 - Edit with a date and clearExpiry

request.description:
A contradictory request: it asks to set an expiry and to remove one at the same time. Rejected at the boundary, so the service is never handed an instruction it would have to guess at.

The service still resolves it deterministically - clearExpiry wins - and a unit test pins that, because a public method has to behave predictably even when something calls it without validation in front.

No token, 200. Authorization covers the mutations and the management read; it never covers the symbol or the redirect.

If this request ever needed a header, every printed QR code in the world would have stopped working.

The management read is behind the token because it exposes the destination and the visit count, which is what a competitor would want from someone else's campaign.

The code itself is not secret - it travels in the short URL - so a public identifier can never be the credential that protects it.

item.name: 38 - Upload a logo with a wrong token

request.description:
The upload authorises before it reads the bytes, so a rejected caller costs no image decoding. That ordering is the cheap defence against someone firing large files at the endpoint without a token.

The service authorises again when it attaches the logo. The repetition is deliberate: the endpoint is correct even if the controller's early check is ever removed.
